grades.quote: One millisecond of processor time is spent each time the processor switches
grades.reason: Exercise set only. Exercises 2.3 and 2.4 pose scenarios with thread-switching cost and response time, but the passage never explains why frequent switches help response time and hurt throughput.

grades.quote: For example, frequent context switches, which are bad for throughput, may be necessary to optimize response time.
grades.reason: Directly answers the question. It says frequent context switches hurt throughput but may be needed for response time. It explains the tradeoff: running one thread sooner means another event's thread waits. It adds the email example and the SJF rationale.

grades.quote: First, the context switching rate goes way up; instead of one context switch per time slice, there is now one context switch per attempt to acquire the popular mutex. The overhead of all those context switches will drive down the system throughput.
grades.reason: Shows that a high context-switch rate from the convoy phenomenon lowers throughput because of switching overhead. It does not address how switching improves response time, so it covers only the throughput-cost side.
Figures and a table that list scheduling goals and mechanisms. They name throughput and response time as goals but say nothing about context switches or why the two goals trade off.
